subsubtopic: THE BUDGET-POSITION OF FORMER FINANCE MINISTER-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, according to confirmed reports in this morning's national press, former Liberal minister of finance John Turner consulted on several occasions with the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) on the totally inadequate budget which was presented here last Monday. It appears, therefore, that indexation of income, pensions and family allowances which was originally proposed by the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, is now being disposed of by the Turner/MacEachen team on the hopeful assumption that the inflation rate will fall to a mere 6
per cent within only six months. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Gilchrist):
That if former finance minister John Turner supports the removal of this plan, he should run once again for Parliament and he should therefore urge the Prime Minister to call the long overdue by-elections in three outstanding federal ridings so that the people of Canada will be able to express their clear opinion on his latest removal of full indexation.

speechtext:

It is ironic that tomorrow we will be celebrating Dominion Day in Canada, and yet the very people who fought to keep this country free are being forgotten in their time of need. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett):
That this House instruct the Minister of Veterans Affairs to take immediate steps to raise substantially the annual allowable incomes in respect of the war veterans allowance from their current unacceptable and unrealistic levels.

subsubtopic: ELIGIBILITY OF LEBANESE VISITORS FOR MEDICAL CARE-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I seek unanimous consent of the House on a matter of extreme urgency. The Minister of Employment and Immigration has recently taken action to allow Lebanese visitors to Canada to remain in Canada for an additional year, with a minister's permit to work. Further, Lebanese visitors who have eligible Canadian relatives who can sponsor them, or are able to offer a guarantee of assistance, may also apply for permanent residence without leaving Canada.
While the minister is to be commended for his actions in this regard, many Lebanese visitors to Canada will require normal medical care over the next year. The cost to their families will be prohibitive, because their present status does not allow these people to enrol in medicare. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga):
That this House direct the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Minister of Health and Welfare to enact the necessary changes in the regulations to allow these people coverage under medicare so that when the need arises for medical attention the Lebanese people visiting Canada will not be unfairly treated.

subsubtopic: IMPACT OF BUDGET ON OLD AGE PENSIONS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, tomorrow we celebrate Canada's 115th birthday and pay our tribute and respect to the thousands of elderly citizens whose effort and dedication in past years helped provide a
better future for us all. Yet in Monday night's budget, grabbing even more of the taxpayers' money to throw away on its disastrous economic policies, the government ignored the financial plight of many of our senior citizens who do not receive the Guaranteed Income Supplement, and announced plans to raise the personal income taxes of this group. These people who, while working hard for our future comfort, set aside a meagre amount of money for their own, should not be so shabbily punished. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That the Minister of Finance, in tribute to this group of very special Canadians on the eve of Dominion Day, immediately announce his intention to rescind the tax penalty on all Canadians receiving the old age security pension.
They worked hard for our security. We should protect theirs.

speechtext:

The minister will obviously know that on Monday night in the budget speech the Minister of Finance indicated or left the impression that there was to be $750 million allocated for job creation. Indeed, in his own speech on the budget yesterday, the Minister of Employment and Immigration said the following about job creation:
It is for that reason that the budget of this government has put $2.3 billion on the table which will create in immediate, direct term 200,000 jobs.
He also said:
Oral Questions
There is an increase of $450 million for direct job creation; that was put in the budget last night.
Those statements and those numbers are clearly misleading and, in my view, intentionally confusing. I would like the Minister of Employment and Immigration to stand now and confirm to this House that his department received $100 million for direct job allocation for this year and not $2.3 billion, not $750 million, and not $450 million. Will he do that now?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: -he will find that the increase in expenditures year to year is significantly less than 20 per cent. I would remind the hon. member, in making these comparisons, that when he uses the national accounts he is bringing into the total expenditures items such as the oil compensation charge which is then offset by compensation payments. When netted out, the total outlays are reduced, as they ought to be.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. We on this side of the House welcome any measure that will assist small businesses in terms of development. But I point out to the minister that on November 12 last year he brought in a provision with respect to capital cost allowance which has done more to prevent retooling and has dried up cash flow. If the minister is serious about resuscitating small business and if he wants to give a signal to the business community, will he consider repealing- which he did not the other night-the capital cost allowance provision in his budget of November 12, 1981?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, Madam Speaker, I could not possibly repeal overall the capital cost allowance.
Why not? You have repealed everyting else.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
If accepted, that would be a further large addition to the deficit which hon. members opposite have been complaining about in their last several questions.
Oral Questions
Cut government advertising and the Minister of Justice.

Madam Speaker, 1 point out to the minister that when businessmen and women of Canada are going broke it is very difficult for them to expand and develop.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of Finance. I think the minister will admit, as he did to my colleague, the hon. member for Bruce-Grey, that when there is no tax room banks are not lending money under the Small Business Development Bond Program. speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the small business bond is in effect and is available from financial institutions which still have tax room available. Their ability to finance these loans will increase as repayments on previously granted loans take place as well.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF WAGE CONTROLS ON CANADIAN NATIONAL AND CANADIAN PACIFIC AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board. He will know that Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railways bargain as a unit with railway unions. My question is this: how will the government's policy of 6 per cent and 5 per cent wage controls in 1982 and 1983 respectively for Crown corporations affect collective agreements recently signed by CN and CP with railway unions? Will the completed bargaining on behalf of CN workers be respected by the government, or will we have a situation in which CN workers
18948

June 30, 1982
Oral Questions
will be getting only a 6 per cent increase in 1982, that is to say, half the increase received by Canadian Pacific workers in 1982, or will it affect 1982 at all? 1 wonder whether the minister could clarify this question for us. speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF WAGE CONTROLS ON CANADIAN NATIONAL AND CANADIAN PACIFIC AGREEMENTS
speechtext:

Clearly an agreement which is in existence will be respected.
As to the additional consideration which is raised with respect to joint bargaining, that is a legal question which will have to be addressed in another forum.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: COLD LAKE PROJECT-LOAN MADE TO IMPERIAL OIL

Madam Speaker, the condition of the loan was that it would be repaid if the project proceeded before the end of June this year. June 30, 1982

speechtext: When an incompetent minister blows $40 million of taxpayers' money, the honourable thing to do is to resign. If he does not believe that, perhaps he could consult with his visiting colleague from Great Britain.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same minister. speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

subsubtopic: DELAY IN FINALIZING CONTRACT
speechtext:

Our construction company is at a standstill, our men have all received their records of employment and so we are becoming a statistic. All happening because a contract that was being organized last August, signed by us and the Fountain Indian Band in January and left to collect dust in the Vancouver DIA office till now it is at this point such a mix-up that we have been informed that the job is not forthcoming.
Is the minister determined to discourage and destroy both the companies and the Indian bands in question in these agreements?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: DELAY IN FINALIZING CONTRACT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, what wide-sweeping, ridiculous conclusions the hon. member has come to; they are beyond any reason. If he cared to indicate the name of the firm which says that it submitted a bid for a contract which was not given to it, I would be pleased to look into it. If he would care to indentify the letter, I will try to find where it is on my "desk".

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same minister. The company is Varian Construction; the minister can find it on his desk. The letter continues:
Some of the people at the Vancouver branch DIA have done more damage than good and we feel this is not only detrimental to our company but very much so to our native Indian people.
In the interests of protecting the officials of the Department of Indian Affairs in Vancouver, will the minister sacrifice the companies in question?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do know that there are many hundreds and, indeed, thousands of relationships between small business contractors, chiefs and band councils, as well as my officials, from coast to coast. I have very seldom heard of any type of bitter complaint of contractors. They are doing business on an ongoing basis with Indian bands and my department, year in and year out.
If there is anything particularly irregular about this matter, or if there have been delays, I will check into it and advise the hon. member. But I am certainly not prepared to come to conclusions of his kind, which attack public servants who cannot speak for themselves, without at least having an opportunity to check the facts, and that is what I propose to do.

turn to the Minister of Employment and Immigration who may know that at the same time B.C. Oh, oh!

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):

-officially, in response to inquiries. Perhaps journalists get better answers from officials than Members of Parliament get from this minister in the House of Commons.

Madam Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order. Earlier today I had an opportunity to read last night's Hansard. You will note that at page 18923 during the speech of the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), the hon. member made a statement which I am sure to everyone who was listening would be quite unacceptable and would no doubt be recognized as untrue. However, I note that Hansard picked up a comment that I made from my seat in which I said "That's a lie". No matter what my opinion of it may be, 1 recognize that to be unparliamentary and I withdraw it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for his withdrawal.

maintopic: MR. STEVENS-REMARKS OF MR. YOUNG AND MR. DEANS
MR. STEVENS-REMARKS OF MR. YOUNG AND MR. DEANS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my point of order, of which I gave your office notice, touched in part on the matter raised by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans). I was also in my point of order going to draw Your Honour's attention to a similar remark made by the hon. member for Beaches (Mr. Young). The actual exchange, as the member for Hamilton Mountain has indicated, appears at page 18923 of Hansard.
At that time I was indicating that the New Democratic Party had been instrumental in encouraging the government to get into the spending program and into the deficit position that it is now regretting, and that this should be drawn to the attention of all Canadian voters. At that time the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain said, "That's a lie". The hon. member for Beaches said, "That's a lie". The hon. member for Beaches also said "It is a plain, outright lie". Hansard then records the following:

maintopic: MR. STEVENS-REMARKS OF MR. YOUNG AND MR. DEANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is funny when you hit the quick-

maintopic: MR. STEVENS-REMARKS OF MR. YOUNG AND MR. DEANS
speechtext: Tell the truth.

maintopic: MR. STEVENS-REMARKS OF MR. YOUNG AND MR. DEANS
speechtext: If you know it.

maintopic: MR. STEVENS-REMARKS OF MR. YOUNG AND MR. DEANS
speechtext:
When you hit the quick, it is always interesting to see . .. how the rabbits come out ot their burrows so fast.
I have consulted Beauschesne. I find at page 108 of Beaus-chesne there are no less than 40 instances cited for the use of the word "lie". On all occasions it has been found an unparliamentary expression. 1 would point out two particularly relevant times when this matter has been raised. At page 1593 of Hansard for December 2, 1976, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is recorded in Hansard as saying:
However, it would be helpful if in the meantime members opposite did not smuggle in lies and falsehoods.
The Speaker at page 1646 of Hansard for December 3, 1976, stated:
The argument that was put forward by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants yesterday was that the use of the words "lies" and "falsehood" constituted unparliamentary language. It is always difficult for the Chair to have to decide on the interpretation of language.
The clear precedent of the past is that even though there are always shades of meaning which tend to excuse the use of such language, when such language was used in the past it was found to be unparliamentary, and rather than getting into an interpretation of shades of meaning it is a safer course to take it as a danger signal and when that kind of language is used it must be withdrawn.
I would cite your own ruling, Madam Speaker, of June 16 in this House when there was a similar comment. You said: "It's an absolute, it must be withdrawn."
In view of that, Madam Speaker, I hope you will find that the expressions as they appear in Hansard are totally unparliamentary and that you will request the members to withdraw them.

maintopic: MR. STEVENS-REMARKS OF MR. YOUNG AND MR. DEANS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 withdrew my comment prior to the hon. member rising. I do, however, wish to bring to Your Honour's attention, since you have been asked to look into this matter, that the quotation the hon. member read is not complete. The hon. member was not drawing attention only to the high level of expenditure of the government and borrowing. He went on to say, and he failed to quote this:
-and the high interest structure the NDP is virtually insisting should be put in place.
That is what I said was a lie.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. STEVENS-REMARKS OF MR. YOUNG AND MR. DEANS
speechtext: Order. I believe the hon. member is now entering into debate on the speech itself. I recognize that those words are unparliamentary. The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain did withdraw them. I believe there was an indication that the hon. member for Beaches (Mr. Young) also used those words. Perhaps he would like to take the floor at this time and withdraw.

maintopic: MR. STEVENS-REMARKS OF MR. YOUNG AND MR. DEANS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I too was on my feet at the same time as the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Sinclair) who was anxious to get up and repeat his own rhetoric of last night. However, recognizing that the language is unparliamentary, I also withdraw, although I recognize that what the hon. member had to say at the time was certainly not true.

maintopic: MR. STEVENS-REMARKS OF MR. YOUNG AND MR. DEANS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. STEVENS-REMARKS OF MR. YOUNG AND MR. DEANS
speechtext: I have to remind the hon. member that he cannot say indirectly what is not allowed to be said directly. The last part of his sentence should also be withdrawn.

maintopic: MR. STEVENS-REMARKS OF MR. YOUNG AND MR. DEANS
speechtext: Gladly, Madam Speaker.

maintopic: MR. STEVENS-REMARKS OF MR. YOUNG AND MR. DEANS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is a little wriggling and eeling going on over there. There is no doubt that our precedents require a direct, unqualified withdrawal. The hon. member for Beaches (Mr. Young) should
June 30, 1982

state simply and concisely that he withdraws the offensive expression used.

maintopic: MR. STEVENS-REMARKS OF MR. YOUNG AND MR. DEANS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 suppose I have been following and watching the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) too long. I absolutely withdraw, Madam Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. STEVENS-REMARKS OF MR. YOUNG AND MR. DEANS

Madam Speaker, 1 rise today, rather significantly, with respect to a question on the Order Paper in my name, No. 4,120. It has been on the Order Paper since March 9, 1982 and remains unanswered. I bring it to the attention of the parliamentary secretary, particularly in light of the question posed today to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) by my colleague from Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker)in which he indicated that there had been a directive by the President of the Treasury Board which in effect would give a preferential wage increase to exempt staff and political staff of ministers of the cabinet of the country.
I am just wondering about the budget which was brought down asking Canadians to restrain themselves to the extent of 6 per cent increases in salaries. My question, Madam Speaker, deals with the practice which releases an undertaking by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) to use Crown corporations and other forms of emoluments for exempt staff, to circumvent the guidelines with respect to salaries for the exempt staff of ministers and thereby in another way circumvent the restraint that one would expect from a Canadian government under such attack for its profligate spending ways. The question, Madam Speaker, is not a difficult one to answer. I simply bring it to the attention of the parliamentary secretary. The question is as follows:
1.	For each Cabinet Minister, what are the names of executive assistants and other members of exempt staff who are receiving income from sources other than from funds allotted to ministerial budgets?
2.	What are the names of those who receive income, favours, loans or other benefits of value from sources other than those permitted by the conflict of interest guidelines for Cabinet Ministers and former Cabinet Ministers?
3.	Did the Prime Minister supply every cabinet minister, every executive assistant and all members of the exempt staff with copies of the "Code of Ethics" produced by the late Prime Minister Pearson and with a copy of the conflict of interest guidelines for Cabinet Ministers and former Cabinet Ministers?
If the parliamentary secretary were doing his job, he certainly would have this question answered. This is not the first time I have brought to his attention the fact that he is attempting to delay answering this question until this session prorogues.

June 30, 1982
Business of the House

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we shall vote on the New Democratic Party's subamendment later today, and after this second day of debate on the budget, we shall resume debate next week on Monday, when we come back after Canada Day and the weekend. Monday will be the third day of debate on the budget. Tuesday will be the fourth day, and a second noconfidence vote will be on the motion proposed by the Progressive Conservative Party. Wednesday will be the fifth day of the debate on the budget and Thursday the sixth, with a final vote on the motion concerning the budget. That is the order of business for next week, unless circumstances dictate otherwise. This may happen, as I explained to my fellow House leaders, when, after discussion, they have examined the bill or bills that were introduced and that arise from the budget, and if we manage to agree on how to proceed with the bill or bills, we may have to change the order of business for next week, starting after Tuesday. As far as Monday and Tuesday of next week are concerned, that is final. Unless there is agreement otherwise at our level, Monday and Tuesday will be two of the days for debate on the budget. Obviously, we still assume Monday will be the third day and Tuesday the fourth day of the debate on the budget.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise with respect to two matters. One relates to what the governent House leader has just said. My understanding is that Monday will be what is normally called "leaders' day". I just hope that understanding holds.
The second matter 1 want to raise is this: the government House leader will be aware of the study conducted by several members of the New Democratic Party into pollution in the Great Lakes, and Lake Ontario in particular, and of the meetings which they held. There has come to light a situation whereby traces of dioxin have been found in the human tissue of the bodies of individuals in Kingston, Ontario. I wonder if the government House leader might give some consideration to a special reference, which we would support, of the matter of toxic waste and its disposal to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry in order that the committee might look into this entire matter and determine whether there are recommendations which might be made, given the severity of the problem and the difficulty we are encountering in dealing with it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have 28 minutes afforded to me. I started last evening and took two minutes. I want to spend some time speaking about the budget.
The budget does not begin to address the problems that confront by far the vast majority of Canadians. The budget has attempted, in a piecemeal way, to put forward some proposals which, I assume, are intended to deal with the unemployment situation that confronts us in Canada, to deal with the very high interest rates that confront us in Canada, to deal with the massive deficit that confronts us in Canada, to deal with the problem of inflation, which is undoubtedly a problem which must be grappled with, and to deal with the lowest dollar value in Canadian history.
Had the government been serious about the problems of this country, it would have recognized right away that the single most difficult and vexing problem that Canadians who are working have to deal with, is meeting their mortgage interest cost. The high level of interest being charged on mortgages is usurious by almost any standard that could have been applied up until 1980. The government should have dealt directly and forthrightly with the problem of high interest rates for people faced with trying to provide their families with a decent place to live at a cost they can afford.
Had the government been serious about the economic dislocation that occurred in businesses, large and small, and about the cutbacks in employment, it would have recognized that the single largest contributing factor to the unemployment that has occurred from coast to coast is the high interest rates that manufacturers and consumers have been required to carry. This has meant that products manufactured by Canadians cannot be purchased by consumers because they cannot afford to pay the 20, 22 or 24 per cent interest rates they have been faced with.

June 30, 1982
Had the government been serious about the record high level of inflation, it would have recognized that the exorbitant interest rates of the last two years have made a serious contribution to it. It would have recognized that every single commodity that is for sale, every single product manufactured in any part of this country, must of necessity incorporate the high interest rate into its price structure as a cost of doing business. Had the government been serious about reducing the deficit, it would have immediately addressed the problem of high intrest rates which have reduced the purchasing power of Canadians, which have made it virtually impossible for Canadian families to buy a home and which have until now eaten away at wages of people who are attempting to make ends meet. Had the government been serious about the deficit, it would have understood that the single largest contributing factor to the deficit has been the outfall of high interest rates which meant a decrease in consumer purchasing, which meant a decrease in manufacturing, which meant an increase in unemployment, which meant a decrease in the amount of personal taxes paid by the majority of Canadians, which meant an increase in unemployment insurance costs, which meant an increase in the cost of operating government in terms of the necessity to provide social assistance for Canadians unable to find work, and which meant a decrease in the corporate tax payable.
Why has there been such a massive shift in the level of indebtedness of this country and a shortfall in revenue over expenditure from November of last year to July of this year? That has come about because not enough people are working or buying products or paying taxes. The government's policy has been one of the contributing factors to the significant downturn in the economy.
You will recognize on behalf of your constituents, Mr. Speaker, that if the government had been serious about dealing with the economic problems of the country, it would have begun by addressing the exorbitant and usurious rates of interest and the destruction that has flowed from allowing those rates to be charged.
In November last year, some seven months ago, I pointed out to the government the need to address the problems of Canada where they existed and the need to look seriously at measures that could be taken in the House to assist Canadians to get back to work, to assist Canadian families to stabilize their lives, to assist the government in raising the necessary tax dollars to pay the important bills, and to assist the government in designing an economic strategy. At that time I put it to the government that there is one real motivator in the economy that rises above all the others in terms of social and economic impact, and that is the provision of housing to meet the need that has been established from coast to coast.
It has been clearly demonstrated that 220,000 housing units should be built in Canada this year but that no more than
130,000	are to be built, and I suspect that is the absolute maximum. Many Canadians cannot find a place to live-not only a place within their means but any kind of decent accommodation for their families.
The Budget-Mr. Deans
I pointed out to the government that for every single house built, 2.2 to three jobs were created, some on the site and some in the industries that provide the bath tubs, the shingles, the tiles, the eavestroughing and other component parts. If an additional 80,000 units were built, close to 200,000 jobs would be created. If those 200,000 jobs were created now, the rate of unemployment, seasonally adjusted as it always is, although I do not know how you adjust people who are seasonally employed-would decrease from 11.6 per cent to 8.8 per cent. We should build the homes that people need and begin the process of creating jobs. Unemployment would then be brought down to a level which, if not acceptable, would at least be closer to being manageable. If those 200,000 people were put to work building the homes people need, unemployment insurance payments would be reduced by $2 billion per year. That could already have been achieved if the government had paid attention to those of us who are every bit as committed to the future of the country as it is. We would have created
200,000	jobs, we would have reduced the level of unemployment from 11.6 to 8.6 and we would have reduced unemployment insurance payments by $2 billion. Then, by way of federal, provincial and municipal taxes, we would have raised $1.16 billion. What would we have? We would have housing for people and we would have 200,000 people working, building and manufacturing. We would not have to find $2.2 billion for the government to spend. We would have a tax benefit of $1.16 billion as a result of this program. In addition to the well known statistical information which says that every dollar invested in a mortgage is recoverable through the payments, we would have saved the government over $3 billion. I would suggest to those who are still in the House-only a few I know-that when you measure that potential against what the government has offered as an economic recovery plan, you have to ask yourself what in heaven's name is wrong. Why is this government so pigheaded, foolish and blind to the methods available to us to begin that process of rebuilding this country? Why is this government tampering when we all recognize that a massive effort is required?
What does the government's program do? It brings forward a $3,000 grant to first-time home buyers, and first-time or otherwise buyers of new homes built during the current year. What that says is that as long as you dig a hole in the ground by the end of December, 1982, then that house will be eligible for the $3,000 grant some time in 1983. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that when you consider it, it is ludicrous. That does not even begin to address the problem. It does not begin to provide homes for people at a price they can afford. It takes money out of the treasury which will not be recovered. It is the kind of program typical of a government bankrupt of ideas. Let me just tell you, Mr. Speaker, that if a person living in Ottawa wanted to buy a home he or she would find the average price of that home to be $68,500.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not a new house.

June 30, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Deans

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is the average price. The average income in Ottawa is just under $30,000 a year. The strange thing is that with that income you do not qualify for a mortgage on a $68,500 house. Therefore, $3,000 in that kind of situation is absolutely of no help. For the government to offer this up as its answer to the housing crisis is shameful, but then it suggests that somehow or other the introduction of this program, and these other small and piecemeal programs it has brought forward, is the way we are going to get Canada back on its feet. The government suggests this is the way to create the economic impetus to enable us to rise from the ashes of destruction brought about by its policies. It will instil in Canadians the desire and drive to build this country to even greater heights and we are going to be able to give homes to people. The government says that people will be able to find and keep their jobs and earn enough to pay the necessary cost of living. If this is the government's answer, then I ask you: is it any wonder that those of us on this side of the House look at the government with disdain, and feel, as my colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) says, despair?
I do not understand this government's initiatives. I do not know how it expects that people, who the day before the budget was brought in could not afford to buy a car, buy a home or meet their mortgage payments with these high interest rates, will, as a result of this budget and its hidden taxes, be able to meet those commitments once the budget is in place. 1 mean, how can you do those things now that you could not do before if you have less money? How can you possibly expect that there will be a recovery when people are in that kind of situation? I do not understand it. There has to be something missing in the minds of the people who advise this government. How in heaven's name can we expect to have manufacturers back to producing at 90 per cent or 100 per cent of capacity, how can we expect to have people back working on the lines, in the shops and offices, if the money available to be spent on goods and services is to be reduced by $1.3 billion? I say through you, Mr. Speaker, that it defies logic. Yet this government proudly stands up and tells us that this budget is really going to meet the need.
This budget, Mr. Speaker, reduces by $1.3 billion the money available to consumers, people who were struggling along and making ends meet. The government then says that this is somehow or other intended to stimulate industry in such a way, and create purchasing power in such a way, that we will have greater employment, more productivity, more tax revenue, and we will be back to the good old days.
Well, I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that is patent nonsense. That is absolutely false hope. That is the worst kind of chicanery I have seen in years. There is no doubt in my mind that if the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen)-and I have always considered him to be an honourable man-stops to think about it, he must surely understand clearly that you cannot reduce the size of the consumer marketplace and expect to sell more. You cannot restrict people's wages to a level below that of inflation and expect them to be able to buy more. I am sure the end result will be-and I hope I am wrong although I do not see how-that people will buy less because they do not have
the money to spend, and those who manufacture will manufacture less, those who work in manufacturing plants will work less, we will have higher unemployment, and that will mean an even larger burden on those who continue to pay taxes. In addition, the deficit will continue to grow, and in the end we will be faced with virtual bankruptcy.
Now, I put it to the government in the most forceful terms I can that it is not too late. It is almost too late, but there is still time. 1 put to the government that if this government is serious about the future of this country and if this government feels any sense of obligation to the working families from coast to coast in this country who are struggling today, the government will pay heed to their cry. Their cry is as loud in the eastern part of the country as it is in the west. The cry is that we must take steps to bring down the interest rates currently being charged. We must, as an absolute priority, bring that level down to a level that is manageable in order that average income earners can go into the marketplace and purchase those things which their neighbours and friends are making. That is the cry of the people of Canada. That is the cry of the small businessman who just put on his door the notice "Out of business, bankrupt" because he could not meet the short-term high-interest payments that he had to make in order to carry his inventory. That is the cry of the large corporations paying out millions of dollars yearly on interest payments which they can ill afford to pay and which price their products out of the market, making it impossible for Canadians to absorb the productive capacity of the country. That is the cry of those who are locked into mortgages paying 20 per cent or more. They are begging and saying to the government, "Please, we cannot carry this burden any more." That is the problem in this country.
I say to you again, as I said before, that we have the ability to solve this problem. I recognize that building homes for people is not the end-all and the be-all. That is not a panacea for everything, but I want to put to the government that activity is vitally important and it is the single most important motivator of any in economic terms. If we were simply to follow the example I have given, and if the government had followed in November what 1 suggested by putting $2 billion to $3 billion-not necessarily all tax dollars-into building homes, we would not have seen the increase in the deficit from the $10 billion or $11 billion to beyond the $19 billion at which it now stands.
When the government told me in November that we could not afford to spend that money because we did not have it, I said then that was wrong. I said then that this was an investment in the future of Canada, an investment from which we would derive a return both in social and in economic terms, an investment from which we would get every single penny back plus interest. I said then that if this investment had been undertaken in November it would have, by virtue of the statistics that I have given, made it unnecessary in this country to absorb that additional $9 billion worth of indebtedness. I do
June 30, 1982

not understand it. If there is a flaw in it, for God's sake, get up and say so. If there is something wrong with that and it will not work as a means of starting the recovery process, then let someone rise and tell me.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They do not dare.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, it is clear to me that between November and December we wasted an opportunity to put Canadians to work because this government was too blind to the realities. We cannot afford such waste many more times.
What do we need? We need a government worth its salt that is prepared to stand up on behalf of Canadians. To stand up on behalf of Canadians is not asking people earning $12,000 a year to tighten their belts. To stand up on behalf of Canadians is to say that we recognize the major problem. It is the interest rate and we are going to bring it down. It is to say we recognize how to create jobs, and build homes. We recognize that small businesses are not able to carry the burden any longer and we will make sure that in the interim period during the recovery these people are given assistance. It is to say we recognize that farmers who have been attempting for years to make it on a meagre income deserve to be given some additional consideration during this very difficult time, and we recognize that what we invest in Canada today we will reap tenfold in the years to come.
This government's policies are bankrupt. It appears that the government is intending to make the country bankrupt like its policies. I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to anyone who cares to listen that there is another way. There may be more than one way, but the way I am proposing today will work. It will not inflict on Canadians additional tax burdens nor will it require Canadians to tighten their belts. It will not require us to suffer 12 per cent or 15 per cent unemployment. It will not require us to pay high interest rates, which this government has supported over the last three years together with its friends in the Conservative Party. This has to stop, and it has to stop now.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure and indeed a privilege for me to have the opportunity to intervene in this debate on the budget. It has also given me the opportunity to follow the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), for whom I have a good deal of respect on most subjects except for his view of the economy and how it works as well as the solutions that he proposes in the well known tradition of his party, which is to spend our way out of all problems.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not what I said.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He asked what is the road to recovery. He invited someone to stand up and tell him what it is. I would like to spend a few moments doing that this afternoon, and I
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
hope the hon. member will remain in the House for that purpose.
He asked what we can do. He said, "Let us stand up on behalf of all Canadians". I invite him to stand up with us on behalf of all Canadians and support this budget, and particularly to support the restraint measures which are contained in this budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I invite him particularly to support the measures which are designated to bring down inflation and interest rates in Canada at the same time to 6 per cent and 5 per cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You cannot do it and you won't do it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain says that it cannot be done. That, of course, is his privilege.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And you have increased government expense by 20 per cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not think most Canadians would agree with the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain's point of view.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Your policy won't do it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are counting on the good sense, judgment and the commitment of Canadians to stand up and support us in this national crusade about which I will be speaking this afternoon.
My colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) yesterday spoke about the budget in terms of employment opportunities. Today, I would like to spend a few minutes dealing with a number of other aspects of the budget which I consider to be relevant and which I think hon. members, particularly from the party of the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain, will be interested.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And so will the stock market.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The opposition, and I refer to the collective opposition, refers very little to the international slump in which the entire western world finds itself.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It does not affect housing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why is that?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why does it not affect housing?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Why is that? I suppose, as political opportunists, the opposition would like Canadians to believe that all the problems that beset this country and the economy at the present time are the product of the sins, past or present, of this government. If they are to win any respect for their views from Canadians-and nearly all Canadians know better-they have to acknowledge that a good measure or a good part of our problems stems from the international economic situation in which we find ourselves today as members of the industrialized western world.

June 30, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
I would ask the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain: would the market for B.C. lumber be helped a great deal by way, for example, of a housing program in Canada in the absence of a U.S. recovery? Does he seriously believe, or is he seriously putting forward the proposition, that the B.C. lumber market will come back in the absence of a U.S. recovery?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It would be better than it is today.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is he suggesting that larger Canadian domestic markets for such items as copper, lead or aluminum will come back in the absence of an international recovery? Canadian sales of automobiles or our output of finished cars, for example, are they likely to come back in the absence of an international recovery?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If you restrict Japanese imports.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am thinking of a company in my own area, Pratt & Whitney of Montreal. As the hon. member knows, it is a manufacturer of jet aircraft engines. Is it likely to come back in the absence of sales in the United States and abroad?
I am interested in noting a comment by Mr. Jack McArthur in The Toronto Star of June 22. I think he had the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain and some members of the Conservative Party in mind when he said:
Some criticism now is so exaggerated that it's just silly.
Also he said:
Who caused the similar inflations in France, Italy and in Britain? Or the dropping currencies in those and other countries such as Japan, Germany and Switzerland? Who's responsible for the terrible unemployment in the U.S. and in almost every other important western industrial nation?
It wasn't Trudeau and MacEachen and they can't insulate us from those things.
That is a lesson the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain and other opposition members have yet to learn. As I said earlier, their criticisms will be taken more seriously if they deal with the real world. To that extent, opposition criticism of the government without reference to the international circumstances in which we all find ourselves frankly is biased, dishonest and misleading. It gives the people of Canada a very false picture of the real situation and also gives them false hopes that a new government such as theirs could pull rabbits out of the hat and that a magic touch here and there, with a bit more spending on this or that, will resolve all our problems and make them go away.
As hon. members know, this point has been made a number of times by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen)-the understanding of Canadians about the seriousness of the situation in which we find ourselves could be helped immeasurably if hon. members across the floor publicly recognized that we cannot float Canada off the world on some pink, puffy cloud, protected and isolated from our neighbours with whom we have so much trade and such extensive financial links. When the world slumps, so do we, and in particular with the U.S. in recession.
In this period our ability to solve our problems is seriously limited by those facts. We must realize-and if I can get the attention of the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain-that inflation is, has been and continues to be the number one problem of western society. All other serious problems which concern us, such as unemployment and unacceptably high interest rates to which the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain made reference, cannot and will not be satisfactorily resolved until we come to grips with the inflationary issue. Most other western countries, including our principal trading partner, that is the United States, have done a much better job at controlling inflation than we have. I suggest to opposition members of the House that we cannot afford to lag behind any longer.
We have also finally come to learn that in our long and less than successful battle against inflation, we must commence with restraints on our own incomes. There is simply no other way. Every country in the western world has turned to this as a focal point in its efforts to hold down prices. It is absolutely fundamental in our battle against inflation. Along with the need to curtail wages is the growing recognition in many countries that the indexing of wages and benefits is an automatic generator of further inflation. The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain shakes his head; I will give him evidence of that in a moment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am shaking my head at your whole presentation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is not just indexing by contract or legislation which is at fault. We have often been conned by the insidious argument that because wages do not go up more than the rise in the consumer price index, these increases which are less than the CPI somehow do not count in the inflationary equation. This ridiculous argument has been used with considerable success by a number of people in our society and by a number of union leaders. Where there is no productivity improvement, which has been the case in recent years, all wage or benefit increases push prices up sooner or later. They validate inflation. They turn the screw another notch and they simply build inflation further into the system.
There was an interesting article from which I should like to quote several passages in Business Week of June 21. The article dealt with Europe breaking the grip of wage indexation. If the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain has not seen the article, I would be more than delighted to send along a copy of it, but in the meantime I should like to read several passages into the record. It reads:
On June 1 the Confindustria, Italy's major employers' association, abruptly revoked its wage indexation compact with the country's trade unions. The action highlights a growing attempt throughout Europe to reverse a decade-long surge in real wages. With more than 10.5 million unemployed, hitherto-docile European corporate officials are turning militant, attempting to squeeze some of the biggest concessions out of trade unions in years.
It continued:
But Italian executives are willing to take the risk of squeezing the unions, in part because the existing wage indexation program is moving the country into an increasingly skewed trading position with inflation-resistant Britain and West
June 30, 1982

Germany. While Italy's wages have risen, pay increases in the other two countries have consistently slowed. This is reducing their inflation and improving trade competitiveness with both Italy and France, which are moving in the same high-wage orbit.
Further on it pointed out that:
-Germany is entering a "virtuous circle" in which low wage settlements are bringing inflation down enough to increase employees' purchasing power despite the pay cuts. And although Britain will not reverse its wage-price spiral to the degree of Germany this year, wage and price increases may come in line in 1983.
It is clear that the experience of European countries is such that everybody benefits when wage demands are reduced and the wage-price spiral is broken.
I suggest that we in Canada must reduce real income. I realize this doctrine is very difficult for some members of the NDP to accept. It is stiff medicine, but it aims principally at the employed people of the country rather than Canadians generally. The weak, the unemployed, the poor and the pensioners are people who must be our first concern, but it is the employed who must pay part of this price. It is certainly the employed-and I number among them members of the House and everyone else, all employed-who must accept the main burden for bringing down wages, the rate of inflation, and of course our deficit.
What happens if wage restraint in the country cannot be effectively achieved? What will happen is more and higher inflation, a dollar continuing to fall and imposing its own price penalties which we have seen, and our deficit rising as we stand to help those in trouble. Why should this burden not be concentrated on the employed of the country as opposed to the disadvantaged Canadians to whom I made reference? Why should that not be done through restraining our own wage demands, those of us who are employed?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why do we not restrain government?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is this too much to ask of Canadians at this time? This is why the government has taken the lead in attempting to break the pattern of wage and benefit increases.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Six per cent across the board, eh?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: For the benefit of all members of this House, I would like to say that we do not like singling out government employees whose pay increases have not been noticeably out of line.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Can we quote you on that?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Please do.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nor do we believe that the recipients of government benefits are less deserving than anyone else in this society. But leadership must begin at home.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Especially the cabinet ministers, right?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It must begin here by those employees who are affected by our own legislation and by our own benefit programs. We are hoping to see the six and five rule and
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
objective which we are introducing adopted by other sectors, by other governments, by other businesses and by the private sector.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are not introducing this program.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Preaching restraint without action on our part, action of the kind we have taken, will not be taken seriously.
For a moment, I would like to turn to the deficit problem. If hon. members opposite were conscious of it before, clearly the response in the marketplace after the announcement of the deficit the other night should make them more aware of the seriousness of our projected deficit of just under $20 billion.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You were aware of it seven months ago.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Both domestic and foreign investors perceive this deficit to be dangerously high-a question mark about our resolve to improve the management of our affairs.
But 1 must say that I was astonished on budget night to see the response of the leader of the New Democratic Party to our proposals. He is undoubtedly the last of the big time spenders, perhaps followed by a few other hon. members of his caucus. 1 have made some rough calculations, but I think my Figures are approximately right, and his proposals to cure all our ills come to something over $5 billion a year. We need this injection of new spending, he alleged, to get the economy rolling.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The pot calling the kettle black. A $20 billion deficit.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would say to the leader of the New Democratic Party that the deficit which was revealed the other night is equivalent to injecting $9 billion into the economy. But where was the applause from the New Democratic Party? I must say that I had expected some excited cheering from the ranks of the New Democratic Party when they witnessed the extent to which the economy has been stimulated during this period.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is their approach. What do we see? Stony silence. Perhaps they are beginning to learn, even at this late date, that this deficit route which they preach is full of pitfalls which will cause great damage. The side effect of some of our restraint measures will help to hold the deficit down by reducing government expenditures-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: To 20 per cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -and adding to our income. But let us look at the reality.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, let us not.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let us look at the reality of 20 per cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The essential attack on the federal deficit and on provincial deficits can only come when people contribute more out of their incomes to reducing them. We have built in

June 30, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
this country one of the best welfare systems in the world, one of which we can all be proud. But we must also pay the bill for that system. That is what I meant when I said that the real incomes of the employed in this country must be reduced so that the capital, which would otherwise go into consumption and into higher and higher wages and prices, into a higher and greater accelerating wage-price spiral so that those resources can be diverted to-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: To ministerial offices and their expenses.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -our society in time of crisis. That is what the budget is doing. The deficit issue is clearly a real one and it is obviously something which cannot be wished away. It can generate a crisis of confidence and it can undermine other actions that we must take. Therefore, we cannot slow our efforts and our approach to bringing it down at every possible opportunity. We must not be seduced into the expansionary spending programs that are foisted upon us, or I should say, preached to us by our friends in the New Democratic Party.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not friends. Please change that. Not friends.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Liberal-NDP coalition.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not friends.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Brothers.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would like to speak for a moment about the program of restraint. The program of restraint has, as its principal objective, the beginning of a national crusade in this country against inflation. The people instinctively know what is needed. Only some of their union leaders and a few others simply do not seem to understand. The people of this country know that inflation cannot be brought down if their pay increases are not cut back. They have learned how the process works by observation. For wage restraint to become a crusade, other governments and businesses must be involved. I must say that it is disturbing to see recent settlements such as 18 per cent for Toronto University professors, or 15 per cent for Toronto metro outside workers. I was reading some comments by Mr. Godfrey.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about MPs, what was their last increase?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Today's Toronto Star states:
Etobicoke Council will likely prove Godfrey's point today by ratifying a 1982 contract giving the borough's outside workers a 15 per cent pay increase.
The union and borough negotiators reached agreement on the 15 per cent raise on Monday night shortly after finance minister Allan MacEachen's plea for economic restraint.
Until then, the union had threatened to go on strike if workers were not given a 17 per cent "catch-up" increase.
"Fifteen per cent is way out of line", said one councillor, "but I guess it will go through because this council had no trouble voting themselves a 14.7 per cent increase effective in November."
The country simply cannot tolerate wage settlements at this level. 1 must say that it is equally disturbing to find most construction workers in the Province of Ontario have been given an increase of $2 per hour. That adds a cost of $4,000 to
the price of the average house. Do hon. members realize what that means in terms of the kinds of housing programs we are trying to introduce? A $2 per hour increase raises the cost of the average house by $4,000.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do you get to the energy agreement?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is surely not the way to control inflation. People in Canada must become seized with the need for wage restraint. They must accept it themselves. They must support our position with regard to union leaders who are extreme in their demands. They must urge their elected representatives, at whatever level, to fight for our 6 per cent and 5 per cent targets so that we will in fact have a rate of inflation of 6 per cent in 1983 and a rate of 5 per cent in the year that follows.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Any bets?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Failing the acceptance of this challenge by the people of Canada, what do we have to fall back on? What would there be? Perhaps mandatory, across-the-board controls which would be difficult to enforce without the kind of support that this crusade is intended to generate. Drift? That is the other alternative. Cruising down the river on a Sunday afternoon? We know that rough water lies ahead and we have already drifted over some rapids. To continue that analogy, drifting-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: For fourteen years!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -always seems to be the easy course until the canoe spills over.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why not call an election on the issue and then we will find out what the people think about it?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The choice is before us. The choice is here for Canadians to make. We on this side are doing our best. We are determined in our efforts to make sure that the reality of the situation in this country is put before the people of Canada.
We would expect, we would hope, and I would exhort the members opposite in their discussions of these very critical issues in this very critical period to make known their own awareness of the depth and universality of this problem to Canadians and to themselves. This is no time for posturing to secure short-term political advantages, even if some of the opportunities look inviting. I hope hon. members of this House will deny themselves those inviting opportunities and raise their sights to the level of the national interest and away from their own partisan interest.
I am saying that the national interest demands a national approach. It demands a national commitment. That is what we seek. Let me quote George Reylea, whose quote appears in yesterday's Ottawa Citizen. When asked to comment on the restraint program, he said:
I don't mind it a bit; it's a hell of a good thing, we should set the example.
June 30, 1982

An unnamed RCMP officer said:
The federal government has got to take a stand some place. This is it.
That is the kind of attitude that we see among our public servants. Perhaps we do not see it among the union leaders. That is the kind of attitude we must see across the public service. I hope that ultimately we will see this kind of attitude across Canada.
These are people with an awareness that is much broader than their own personal interests. I received a telex from Mr. R. S. Hurlbut of General Foods dated June 29. Responding to the plea of the Minister of Finance for voluntary wage constraint in the private sector, he said that General Foods today placed a 6 per cent limit on increases to salaried employees. The program is effective July 1. President Hurlbut said that the federal budget "set the tone for an economic recovery in Canada. Now it is up to business, industry and labour to get behind it and make the program work". He went on to say that "if Canada hoped to regain its competitive place in world markets, inflation must be brought under control. Restoring economic health to this country must become the number one priority of every Canadian".
These people know what the national interest is. It is up to every Canadian, not just Mr. Hurlbut of General Foods who has already begun and is doing his part to make this program work. I hope that what we have seen in the case of General Foods and others who will be following their example and our own is the beginning of an avalanche of support for this program to push that crusade I referred to in my earlier comments.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) in his appeal to have this restraint initiative flow out through and across the various sectors of Canada. The time is long past due where a restraint initiative should have become a part of government policy.
After having listened to the NDP House leader, the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), I wonder why they voted against the budget of my colleague, the minister of finance in the Thirty-first Parliament. When a sincere initiative of restraint was put forward, it was labelled short-term pain for long-term gain. It was rejected by both the Liberals and the NDP. It was the NDP who made it possible for that government to fall. It was their motion. As a result, we now have long-term pain for short-term political gain. We have lived with the abuse of political power ever since that dark night of December 11.
It was the NDP who today appealed for lower interest rates, I believe 1 per cent above the rate of inflation. How they get that magic combination of arithmetic, I will never understand. It was the NDP who voted against mortgage deductibility for the home owners of Canada. That in itself has turned out to be the national tragedy. There is not a member of this House who is not aware of the deep, sincere and pitiful anguish experienced by families in thousands of households across this nation as I speak today.
Our trouble started back in 1968 when we changed the rules of this House and deemed the process of supply to be passed,
The Budget-Mr. Huntington
the estimates on May 31 and the appropriations bill on June 30. That is when the trouble began. There were no longer any checks and balances within this chamber, which is really here for the fundamental purpose of controlling supply and forcing accountability.
Accountability was lost from that day forward. Spending went out of control, as has been reported by Canada's auditors general. It is still out of control. They are profligate spenders. When there were good days of high revenues, they never thought of putting a dollar in the bank to cover the bad days, which always come within business cycles.
In 1968 we were spending something like $692 per taxpayer in this country. Today this government is spending over $8,200 per taxpayer in this country. Today we are spending $3,175 for every man, woman and child in Canada. In 1968 it was $549. Our overspending in this fiscal year alone is $1.66 billion a month. I can remember you, Mr. Speaker, being in the Chair not too many months ago when I used to complain about the overspending being a billion dollars a month. In the last year, this government's spending habits have risen from $1 billion a month to $1.66 billion. This government is spending that much more than it is taking in through revenues.
Something is wrong with the whole federal system. Every single person in Canada feels it, knows it and is worried. Everyone is asking what they can do, how they can help, how to get this in check and how they can bring discipline to their own spending.
Spending is out of control. Not only that, we have been borrowing to pay interest on our borrowing. We have been borrowing as though the only source in Canada that needed funds was the federal government.
In the next six months we face potential maturity on official government debt instruments which amount to 48 per cent of the total marketable debt that this government holds. In case that figure is not sufficiently startling, that is some $443A billion in potential call on the federal government as we appoach closer and closer to a condition of collapse. This is reckless and irresponsible spending for short-term political gain. It is a tragedy. Our democracy is paying for it.
Since this government has been in power the inflation rate has moved from 9.2 per cent to 11.8 per cent, correct at May. The Canadian dollar has slipped from 84.6 cents to under 77 cents today. As to interest rates, the mortgage rate has moved from 14.69 per cent to 19.75 per cent. The unemployment adjusted rate, Mr. Speaker, has gone from 7.6 per cent to 10.2 per cent in May.
I heard the appeal of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) today. I know that gentleman and he is very sincere, in spite of the fact that he was one of the most powerful critics of this government's spending habits prior to becoming a member of the House of Commons. He was the author of that book "Fiscalamity". It laid it all out and said how the

June 30, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Huntington
economy should be corrected, but not one measure in that book has been put into place since he has been a minister.
The Minister of Finance on budget night made an appeal to reduce the inflation rate of this country from 12 per cent to 6 per cent by capping increases, and he was to start with Members of Parliament and the federal civil service. Fie put peculiar emphasis on the word "solidarity" in that appeal.
I have in my hand a copy of the committal order of Lech Walesa, the father and creator of the Solidarity movement in this world. That man was struggling for the people of Poland. He was struggling for their right to join a union. He was struggling for the freedom to choose for the Polish people. He was struggling for the freedom to bargain with employers, even if it was the state. Political freedom was a dream in that land. Mr. Speaker, if you ever want to experience some sober reading, flip through the committal order of Lech Walesa and read the list of places of detention in Poland. They are all listed with the numbers of internees.
As we watch Canada unfold in 1982, more and more people become concerned. When we use the word "solidarity" I hope we can return to a complete understanding of how important that word is to so many people in a country that dreams of the freedom that we have a tendency to take for granted and abuse.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
That is what is happening here today. I say this, Mr. Speaker, in all sincerity, because the form of government in Canada has been changed. Many of us are very concerned about the condition of rules in this House and that it is moving away from a participatory democracy more and more to a leadership form of democracy, where announcements are made outside the Chamber. We have 3,500 orders in council, rules and regulations coming down per year. We are jammed up with details on massive legislation that is all leading us and directing us to one thing, Mr. Speaker, and that is structured intervention in the marketplace.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, we of all people can understand and feel the historic warning that once you lose freedom in the marketplace, all through history people have lost their political freedom.
1 have watched this alliance between the New Democratic Party and the Liberal government, this Liberal-NDP socialist alliance, move in with structure and intervention and control over the marketplace. They move in with an avalanche of Crown corporations. We have just given the minister responsible for the national energy policy powers to put in place, at his will and whim, subject to cabinet approval, Crown corporations with agency of Her Majesty status, which puts them in a place all by themselves. The laws of the provinces, the laws of this federal government, cannot touch these people. These people can commit themselves to debt and to risk, and they create contingent liabilities on top of the burden on this country. The last time 1 checked, our burden was something like $137 billion of direct debt. We now have another $20
billion to add to that. On top of that debt, our Crown corporations' sub-government has created another known $58 billion of contingent liabilities on this government. It is no wonder that some of us at large in this country, including the chief executive officers of banks, are now outwardly and outspokenly concerned about the condition of this country. Countries do go bankrupt, just the same as we are watching small business, medium business and now large business face bankruptcies and receiverships.
Last evening I heard my colleague, the hon. member from Provencher (Mr. Epp), comment on the Minister of Finance's appeal to the country. He pointed out that the trouble the Minister of Finance and his colleague the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) have, is that no one trusts this government. No one believes them any more, because they are a party that can justify anything. When I say a party that can justify anything, Mr. Speaker, back on January 29, 1982 I was in this House with my earphone plugged in, and the member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Gimai'el) told us exactly what a Liberal was and pointed out how easy it is for a Liberal to justify anything.
That brought to mind the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when he wrote in Cite Libre in April, 1963:
The political philosophy of the Liberal Party is simplicity itself; "Say anything, think anything: better still, think nothing but put us in power, for we are best fitted to govern."
Today we have corrected a budget from last November 12 with a deficit projected at $10.5 billion; and some six or seven months later, that projection was out by an obvious 60, 70 or 80 per cent. In fact, I will say 100 per cent, because the deficit is now projected, seven months later, to be $20 billion. Something is seriously wrong.
With this restraint program and the appeal in the budget from the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board to work, you need the trust of the nation. As the hon. member from Provencher (Mr. Epp) last night said: "You have cried 'wolf too often and the people just don't trust you." You have only to go back and look at the question period today to see some of the answers that deliver further mistrust of the government.
In 1968, in the book "Federalism and the French Canadians", the Prime Minister stated:
Federalism must be welcomed as a valuable tool which permits dynamic parties to plant socialist governments in certain provinces from which the seeds of radicalism can slowly spread.
The people of Saskatchewan woke up to that statement and the truth of it.
