In 1968 the Prime Minister promised to hold government interference where it is not needed. What did we have through the last 14 years but a gradual building up, and into the last two years a rapid movement into a structured, totally interventionist federal government, with centralist control over the whole marketplace in the economy of Canada. That is our lot. He said he would not do it; he has done it.
In 1968 this same Prime Minister promised his government would not spend more than it earned. In 1968 the gross debt was $32.5 billion. We do not know what the gross debt is today, but it must be close to $160 billion. The Prime Minister said he would not spend more than his government earned. I heard him.
The 1966 white paper on metrication and the minister who charted the omnibus bill through for the then Liberal government said-and reiterated-that although the implementation dates were not mandatory, they served as guidelines for each member's company or organization in a given sector. Today we have orders in council making metric mandatory. Prison sentences are being imposed or threatened on small merchants and large merchants; it does not matter where. The government wants trust; it has not earned it.
In 1974 the Prime Minister promised not to implement wage and price controls. He said so during an election campaign. He said he would not do it. What did he do one year later? He implemented wage and price controls without a mandate.
In 1974 the Prime Minister promised to rehabilitate passenger train traffic. In 1981, through order in council, 20 per cent of our passenger lines were abandoned. And the government wants trust?
In 1975 the Prime Minister declared there was no way the free market system could be made to work. He added that after wage and price controls were lifted, the government had other tools of control at its disposal. He was speaking of the CTC and the CRTC.
In 1979 the Prime Minister said his government would provide some compromise and some sense of solidarity in federal-provincial relations. During that same election campaign he described himself as a chairman who could reconcile the provinces' differences. What did he do in 1982? He announced the death of co-operative federalism.
In 1980 the Prime Minister campaigned against an 18-cent gasoline tax, an excise tax in the Crosbie budget. What has happened is pitiful history. Even the gasoline and electric light bills of the people of British Columbia have a subtax added to the bottom whereby they are paying for Petro-Canada. Eighty-three cents will be the burden on the Canadian people by the end of 1983, when 18 cents was defeated by the political opportunists of the socialist alliance. I could go on and on and give hon. members chapter and verse as to why this appeal in this hour of need in this country will not reach out. It is because the people do not trust the Liberal Government of Canada.

Right on!

Does this budget address the interest rate problem? No, it does not. If we want one indicator of the emotional level of sophisticated people in the land, we can read the stock market indicators. Activity on the stock market is mostly the result of emotion in anticipation of the future. The day after the budget was known the Toronto Stock Exchange indicator dropped 40 points. That tells us how the knowledgeable people of the country reacted. The dollar opened at 76 cents and climbed back to almost 77 cents.
There are only three ways to bring interest rates down. High interest rates are a national dilemma. Their high level has been caused by the inflationary policies of governments. They have been caused not just by the policies of the Canadian government but by those of governments the world over. When we move away from a currency or monetary system based on something which can be measured against and turn the currency or monetary system of a country over to politicians, it is not long before it is prostituted and destroyed. It is called fiat money, or false money. Our currency is no longer a medium of exchange in this country. It is a commodity, and somehow or other government policies have to address that.
If we are to address the real problems which have developed as we have come out of the Keynesian era of post-war reconstruction, we have to recognize that we have repeated history once again by allowing rigidities to be built into our system. Those rigidities are the result of control over the marketplace by too much corporate concentration. Capitalist units cannot compete. They are exactly the same as states and state bureaucracies. They want control. They cannot be bothered with the rough and tumble of competition and the give and take of the marketplace. So we have allowed massive corporate concentration unparalleled in any other free society or western society to take place in Canada. These capitalist concentrations buy up all the little annoyances in the marketplace and create monopolies. We allow marketing boards to control supply in order to keep prices up and drain the consumer's pocketbook and wallet.
We also have allowed too much power to be concentrated in the hands of organized labour in key segments of the economy. I am not attacking the rank and file of organized labour; organized labour was necessary and good because it had to match and balance the degree of capitalist corporate concentration we had allowed to develop. That offset had to be there. However, as these organized labour units bargain for more and more of the pie, it is very interesting that fewer and fewer people go back to work. I agree with what the President of the Treasury Board said today. Somehow or other we have to deliver on this one. It is just too bad the people of Canada no longer trust hon. members opposite, and in order to deliver they will need a lot of help.
There are three ways to bring down interest rates. One is an economic collapse, and we are coming dangerously close to the end of a business cycle which could collapse. The second one is to use the Bank of Canada more effectively in controlling the flow and taking the heat off the flow of exchanges in and out of Canada. I spoke about that on June 21, as recorded in

June 30, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Huntington
Hansard at page 18680, and I tried to put out some questions which would excite some minds to see if we could not break through the impasse the country's economists have come to in managing our economy more effectively in international monetary systems and marketplaces.
Our dilemma also stems from the 1971 Benson tax act. We have now had a decade of socialist taxation. It is an absolute failure. We cannot enter the GATT era unless we move ourselves back to something which taxes costs instead of the profits and home-generated capital we so desperately need in order to manage, own and control our own affairs. We still have to go out and borrow from other countries which save in order to expand and make use of the vast resources we have in this country. Our taxation system is wrong, and we in this House should be paying a lot of attention to a new taxation philosophy which would allow us to prepare for the GATT era and once again allow this country and its workers, its managers, its professionals and even its politicians to hold their heads high in the industrialized world, because we have slipped to thirteenth place from third.
Something is desperately wrong and we are not addressing the fundamental causes of our problems. They are there. They have to be identified, and then we have to go to work with vital debate in order to solve them. We cannot go on listening to the economists who have turned themselves into a debating society, one on one, each putting the other down. That day has gone. The Keynesian era has gone. The rigidities must be addressed. New taxation policies are needed. This government will not bring them in. 1 am speaking in a canyon here because this government is a structuralist, interventionist, collectivist type of government. It will control, one way or another, everything in the marketplace. There will be no freedom left. I want to go in the opposite direction, and that is the way I want to see my party go.
I am always fascinated when the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) speaks. Many members of the New Democratic Party are good speakers.

They are very fluent and oratorical, and there are some very nice guys down there, too. But we get into trouble with them on their mindset. It pays to listen to the NDP rhetoric.
They have made an appeal to the small business community. In fact, every time they speak they appeal to the small business community. The rhetoric is pretty smooth. I do not think we could start from a more sound base, but the policy of the NDP is diversification away from the strongest element there is in the process of creating wealth. The advertisement reads well. Without jobs and wealth how can we sustain the welfare benefits in our system? If we do not develop the
resources that we are blessed with, how can we create the jobs and the wealth that is needed to sustain the enviable social welfare system that exists in this country?
For the eight years that I have been a member of this House I have been telling the NDP that, if they continue to support the profligate spending of the Liberal government, one day the welfare system that we are so proud of in Canada and that attracts so many people to the country would be threatened with collapse. That day is here, Mr. Speaker.
This ad that I referred to says that the NDP would restructure the FBDB. Mr. Speaker, it has been in the process of being restructured for the last three years. The ad says they would lend money with more reasonable rules on collateral. How is that possible? The FBDB lost $48 million last year and this year its losses will probably amount to $70 million or $80 million. It is the lender of last resort and has to come to this House for very large appropriations. I support those appropriations, Mr. Speaker, because some winners emerge from the system.
The NDP would give small business managerial, financial and marketing advice. What is CASE doing? It is one of the finest consulting services that this government has ever made available to the business community.
The ad talks about an industrial strategy that would de-emphasize the "rip and run" of resource exploration. It says that the NDP wants rent controls. Mr. Speaker, it is interesting that the Marxist activitists are always working against landlords. We have had a period of an almost zero vacancy rate in some parts of Canada.
I have a real feeling for the need for public housing because I could not have started in business if I had not lived in a CMHC house at $49 per month when I was starting out. Today grants are offered but people have to apply for them. This means there is more control over their lives. Business has to apply for grants to drill holes-but only if they are winners. Business and individuals have to apply for funds that should be given in tax points. Two million people making decisions at large in this country is a lot better than having 350 bureaucrats isolated and insulated from the reality of the business place making decisions.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada, along with other industrialized nations, is passing through a period of economic recession. To varying degrees unemployment, inflation, high interest rates and lower productivity are apparent in all industrialized countries.
The fundamental reasons for this widespread recession are varied. Higher petroleum costs have adversely affected the cost of everything else. It is difficult to think of any product which does not require energy in its growth, extraction or manufacture. Increased expenditures by governments dating back to the United States financing of the Vietnam war have exceeded real economic growth. As the public's expectations of what governments should provide have greatly expanded, governments have not always matched their increased spending with increased taxation. Accordingly, deficits have grown and money has been printed, which creates the classic inflationary circumstances of more money chasing fewer goods and services.
Canada has not, of course, been immune from these and other international economic misfortunes, and Canada has responded in ways similar to those of other western countries. We have reduced our money supply, we are absorbing substantially higher energy prices, we have sought ways to reduce federal government expenditure.
On the question of restricted money supply, the Business Council on National Issues recently endorsed the government's policy by saying:
We have nothing but admiration for the battle being waged in the name of common sense with respect to the Bank of Canada's monetary policy. There is really not much point in validating with increased money supply the very inflation that must be reduced.
Excessive money supply is not, of course, the only element which must be addressed resolutely in attempting to reduce high inflation and interest rates. However, in introducing broader policies to reduce inflation and interest rates as the sure route to more jobs and real prosperity, Canada is in a more vulnerable position than most other industrialized countries. About one-third of our gross national product, indeed our very prosperity, if you will, depends upon exports; a much higher percentage than most countries.
Further, about 70 per cent of those exports are to the United States. That fact alone makes us especially vulnerable to economic policies pursued by Washington. We are rendered even more vulnerable by the fact that of our trade with the United States, more than one-half is really intracompany

June 30, 1982
The Budget-Mr. MacLaren
transfer; that is, products or components moving among the plants or warehouses of a single company.
Over the years we have from time to time heard about how, when the United States sneezes, Canada catches a cold, or about the twitchy elephant and its wary bedmate, the mouse. Such metaphors, while colourful and excessive, do have some validity. The U.S., while having achieved some success in reducing inflation, has done so at the expense of massive unemployment. Also, the U.S. although remained incapable of reducing its own interest rates, with its federal government deficit seen as a major factor contributing to the upward pressure on interest rates. If interest rates in Canada were lower than those in the United States, money would naturally flow out of Canada in search of the higher rate of return.
As Canadian dollars were sold to purchase U.S. dollars, the exchange rate of the Canadian dollar against the U.S. dollar would decline. Our imports, largely paid in U.S. dollars, would cost more, as would the repayment of interest and principal on past borrowings. Inflation in Canada would grow as a result. An alternative, in theory, would be to impose currency controls; but if Canadians wish to maintain an open boundary for currency exchange with the country with whom we do so much trade and which has so heavily invested in Canada, then controls to retain capital in Canada are simply not an option.
While we must, apparently, anticipate that interest rates will remain high in the U.S., at least until Congress and the President resolve their current differences over the size of the deficit, there are some things that we can realistically do to increase our own productivity and reduce our inflation and interest rates. The new budget introduces or strengthens a variety of such measures. Other opportunities reside in such concurrent government initiatives as a national program for occupational training, increased export promotion, and more regulatory reform. However, the possibilities for improvement by all such measures are unfortunately limited by an inescapable fact, which again the business Council on National Issues has stated succinctly:
We cannot and will not return to strong economic growth as long as our major trading partners continue to experience slow growth or stagnation. Canadians' expectation of what can be achieved must be realistic.
This is a truism that Canada and other western nations took to the recent Versailles Summit meeting when they sought modifications of current U.S. economic policies. But it is a statement of cold comfort to the 1.2 million Canadians now unemployed or those who are facing business bankruptcy or farm foreclosure.
To lessen the adverse impact of economic policy pursued elsewhere, we in Canada must achieve more singleness of purpose here at home. Our prosperity in the past has allowed us to afford the luxury of differences between federal and provincial governements which has lessened our ability to define national directions.
Equally, we have allowed ourselves the luxury of an adversary relationship among labour, business and government. Several of our major trading competitors have, in contrast, achieved a harmony of national intent not evident in Canada.
Accordingly, I welcome the initiative of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to bring together today the provincial Premiers in an effort to ensure that the two levels of government practise the same restraint, that they march to the same economic tune.
Equally, the refinement of much needed measures to encourage investment by Canadians in productive capacity- not in consumption but in productive capacity-will be recommended by a national committee composed of eminent businessmen, economists and financial experts. This should in turn reinforce consultation and understanding between at least two of the major forces in our economy.
If greater cohesion of national purpose results from these and other initiatives, Mr. Speaker, the probability will be enhanced of Canadians placing themselves in a position to compete effectively when international economic recovery does come.
The economic problem confronting Canadians today is not, after all, a short-term one, however difficult and painful for many those short-term problems may be. There is also the longer-term problem of ensuring that our inflation is sufficiently reduced for us to be able to compete against those who have already achieved such reduction. We must ensure that we do not price ourselves out of world markets.
Canada is not in such a position today, Mr. Speaker. Typically, wage settlements in Canada, including those in the federal and provincial public service, have run well ahead of a number of our major trading competitors during the past few years. Further, our income expectations have considerably exceeded our limited productivity increases. When that happens more inflation and more unemployment inevitably result. Canadians must accept lower income increases if such increases are to match increases in our productivity. This must happen if we are to compete with those in other countries who have achieved a greater equilibrium between increases in their income and their productivity.
Such restraint is now becoming evident elsewhere even in the United States, our major trading and investment partner. That is why in the budget the federal government has shown the way to breaking the wage-price spiral, breaking what is frequently called inflation psychology. The federal government could, of course, impose mandatory wage and price restraints on the whole economy, but that is a Draconian intervention which can be avoided if the example now set by the federal and some provincial governments is followed by the private sector. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) stated in his budget speech:
This strategy will lead in the short run to a lowering of our real income.
There is no escaping that unpalatable fact. The minister added:
But it will soon slow the process that is eroding our pay cheques. It will check the rise of unemployment. And it will establish a firm basis for the resumption of real income growth throughout the economy.
June 30, 1982

Income restraint in the federal and provincial public sectors will set not only an example for voluntary action by the private sector-and it is the private sector which has itself advocated voluntary action and not mandatory controls-but it will also release funds to stimulate more private investment in productive capacity. Such funds are not, however, adequate in themselves to enable the federal government to provide necessary investment incentives and to encourage an early return of greater business confidence.
At the same time as the government limits wage increases to 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent next year for a half million federal and Crown corporation employees, it will place similar limits on the indexing of major social programs, exempting those recipients, however, who are in the greatest need. Equally, the government will move on the other side of the equation. It will limit indexing of income tax to the same 6 per cent and 5 per cent formula. And price increases under federal regulatory agencies will also be limited by the same amounts. This whole package, when taken together, will contribute to a national goal of reducing substantially our current high rate of inflation and of regaining our growth momentum.
This package sets for the provinces and the private sector a common goal of no more than 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent next year in those areas of income prices under their control. To succeed, this must be a truly national effort. The national government has now shown the way to move, as the finance minister has noted, from the 12 per cent world of recession to the 6 per cent world of recovery.
This action in itself will contribute to a growing realization in our business community that the federal government deficit will be both constrained and increasingly used in a positive, constructive manner. Investor confidence will be enhanced. Government revenue will be released which, when diverted into incentives for productive investment, can reinforce the mood of greater investor confidence and, in turn, generate greater tax revenue as well as creating badly needed jobs. The private sector is, after all, the principal motivator of the economy, the principal employer of Canadians as well as the generator of prosperity.
It is for this reason that the reduction in government spending is being used in two ways, both directly and indirectly to reduce the deficit and to promote more productive investment.
Some direct measures are immediate. Others are for final decision this autumn but will be retroactive to the date of the budget. When I speak of immediate measures, I have in mind, for example, those relating to the housing industry. The government proposes a $3,000 non-taxable cash grant to all purchasers of new houses for which construction starts before December 31 and first-time buyers of existing houses purchased up to December 31. Some members opposite have argued that such a grant will do nothing to promote the construction industry in particular or the general investment climate in general. This measure is, in fact, an unprecedented aid to help both home buyers and the construction industry.
The Budget-Mr. MacLaren
For example, many Ontario residents can now combine the federal grant of $3,000 with the $5,000 interest-free loan provided by Ontario. Accordingly, the vice-president of the Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada said that:
This is a very good attempt, especially with the Ontario program-no one can ignore a combined grant of $8,000-it is a good short-term stimulus and we'll look after the long-term ourselves.
The vice-president of the Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada suggested that approximately 30,000 more new houses would be built this year because of these incentives. Thus the incentives not only illustrate the importance of existing federal-provincial co-opertion in the economic field, but also suggest the benefits that the construction of new houses will bring to the Canadian economy as a whole.
When coupled with provincial grants, it is projected that as many as 100,000 new home buyers will take advantage of the scheme. Moreover, the federal grant program is estimated to create 50,000 new jobs in the construction industry alone. Undeniably, such stimulus by government is good for the hard hit construction industry and for the economy generally.
In speaking of immediate measures, I also have in mind such initiatives as the new investment grants to small business, which have been outlined in the budget, the postponement of the dividend tax on small business and the taxation of interest income. Foreign investment review procedures will be streamlined to avoid delays and red tape that have hindered efforts to ensure that Canadians receive maximum benefits from foreign investment. Increasing the threshold for mergers and acquisitions by non-Canadian investors can, for example, bring new opportunity for increased productivity in our economy.
All these and other direct and immediate measures contained in the budget are in a sense bridging mechanisms leading to yet more substantial measures in the time ahead. The budget's more indirect and more fundamental method to encourage investment is based on the fact that current Canadian savings are at levels substantially ahead of several of our major competitors. Our capital markets cannot, however, channel these substantial funds into productive investment when inflation so grossly distorts real earnings. The attractiveness of investing in common shares to provide companies with the funds essential for renewal or expansion are simply not there when inflation distorts the measurement of income from capital. As the valuable document tabled on Monday night entitled "Inflation and the taxation of personal income" states:
Inflation-induced increases in interest rates can lead to cash flow problems for borrowers and can hamper the proper functioning of the capital markets. These problems have become particularly acute for home buyers and for many businesses contributing to the depth of the current recession in a number of industries. At the same time, the tax treatment of investment income has left many investors facing negative real after-tax rates of return on their savings in spite of higher interest rates.
Accordingly, the government has put forward tax proposals that would remove some of the distortions caused by inflation. These proposals are designed to provide for more appropriate

June 30, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Blenkarn
taxation of interest income and capital gains from selected investments by individuals. The committee of businessmen, economists and financial experts which was announced on Monday, during the next three months, refine the measures intended to result in new incentives for investment. These include a registered shareholder investment plan, an imaginative step which, by offering a shelter for investors, will make available substantial additional funds for productive investment. Companies which have found that their traditional sources of investment capital have dried up in the face of inflation and high interest rates will have new funds to invest in the new plant and equipment which we need so urgently to improve our industrial productivity. In welcoming this initiative of the Minister of Finance, the president of the Investment Dealers' Association stated: "His diagnosis of what we have to do in Canada is correct: improve productivity and confidence."
A second major step to improve productivity and confidence will be to create a new form of term deposit. Tax on interest earned on such deposits would not include that part which merely reflects the rate of inflation. With such an incentive, buyers of new homes would be able to obtain mortgages at 3 to 6 percentage points lower than prevailing rates. Loans for new investment would be available at the same reduced rates to farmers, fisherfolk and small businessmen. Here again is a major new opportunity to channel Canadian savings into Canadian productive capacity and into improved productivity which, when matched with wage restraint, will place Canada in a position to compete effectively in world economic recovery.
In accordance with the widespread desire across Canada that major tax reforms be discussed publicly, the Minister of Finance offered proposals for such consultation in his recent green paper. The decision to refer the major proposals which I have just described to an expert committee and to invite public comment by the end of August is fully in accord with the new, more open approach to budget-making. The need for prompt action will, however, be as evident to members of the committee as I am sure it is to every member of the House.
Measures to increase productivity are, after all, the only real panacea for inflation. However, they will only succeed if we have the collective will, unity and determination to reduce our inflation. I do not doubt that Canadians have that will and that determination and that the new budget shows the way forward. Supplementary programs and additional measures such as 1 have already mentioned will also be necessary, but as a result of the new budget the course is now clearer.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel sad for my country today. Our economy is in terrible shape. Businesses are failing. We have heard evidence before the committee of the House on banking and bank profits and we now have the extent of the recession or depression, if one wants to call it that.
When we look at our country, we look at the fact that we have enough oil in Hibernia, in the tar sands and in already known heavy oil deposits to last for more than 200 years. Also we have gas, coal, hydro, uranium and energy of all kinds. Yet we are prevented from exporting that energy and developing that energy for export by a foreign investment review policy and a foreign policy promulgated by the New Democratic Party and certified by the government to ensure that we fail to develop the resources and the potential of the country and fail to supply our people with jobs.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are against the National Energy Program.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are in favour of the foreign investment review process and you want to ensure that people do not have jobs. You want to keep people out of work.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Baloney.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are the same type of party as the party opposite.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You have voted with them twice as much as we have.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have a non-confidence motion today. It is an amendment by those people to my left to the motion we have put forward. They are trying to trap us and ensure that we will not vote against the government, that we will vote with the government. I want to tell my friend, because he is the only member of that party who is present in the House, that we will vote against the government. We do not care what kind of a fool motion his party puts up because his party is irrelevant. It is irrelevant to the workers of Canada; it is irrelevant to Canadians generally. It will not be long before there are very few of them here.
As 1 was saying, we in this country have more resources, more water, more available arable land, more fishery resources, more timber resources, more minerals of every kind and more literate people than any nation of the world. Yet we have one of the most serious depressions we have ever faced since the 1930s. Perhaps it is as serious as, or even more serious than the one of the 1930s.
Our gross domestic product has declined 5.1 per cent in the last 12 months. We have a situation where the government comes before the House of Commons with a budget deficit of $20 billion. We have a situation where we have a banana dollar at 77 cents. 1 ask why we have 11.8 per cent inflation. Why do we have a million and a quarter people unemployed? Why do we have interest rates 2 to 5 percentage points above those in the U.S.A.? Why do we have a lack of confidence in Canada? Why do we have people in Canada who are unable to find jobs when we have assets that any other nation or people in the world would be absolutely jealous of?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Conservative policies.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hear the hon. member. I remind him that he is a member of the no-hope party. It is called the New
June 30, 1982

Democratic Party, but it is the no-hope party. It is a party which looks after the welfare of people-a welfare party is what it is. It wants to put everyone down to the lowest common denominator. It wants to put everyone in blue jeans, so that they will all be equal and they will all march to the socialist drum. This is what they offer the people of Canada, no future or hope.
It is surprising that the government across the way has accepted their philosophy. Perhaps it is not too surprising. After all, was it not the leader of the government who was an active campaigner for the socialists in the 1962 election and in the 1963 election? Was he not a member of that party who worked so hard for socialist philosophies then and found that the only way to make socialism really work was to join the Liberal Party, because they would then have a base on which to put socialism in charge of Canada?
There once was a Liberal Party, the Liberal Party of Laurier. It was a Liberal Party which said that Canada would be the country of the twentieth century. Would Sir Wilfrid Laurier, as the Liberal leader, have said: "Lower your expectations, lower your hopes, lower your chance to build a profitable business, lower your chance for a better home, lower your expectations; don't go for a better job or more money to get ahead and build your family"? Are those the kinds of things we would have heard from Laurier as leader of the Liberal Party? No, not on your life.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nor from St. Laurent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My friend says "Nor St. Laurent". Nor Mackenzie King, even. But what do we hear from this party opposite in its budget address? "Lower your expectations".
Then it is wondered why we have not used our Canada to its great potential. We find the answer in the minister's budget address, on page 2, in the second paragraph, where the minister complains about foreign governments and says:
Their governments are unable, or have not chosen, to design their economic policies to help us get out of our recession.
Well, there you are. A banana republic we surely have become, because now we hear the government saying that foreign governments have not organized their affairs to help us get out of our recession. Well, should they? Should we, with our inherited assets in this great land occupied by about 24 million people, be looking to foreign governments, to foreign countries, to be bailing us out of the recession?
1 asked the minister just that type of question in the House the other day, on June 16. With respect to the question of confidence in Canada, the minister said in reply to me that I was responsible for undermining the confidence of the investment community. He said, as reported at page 18514 of Hansard'.
I would suggest to him that he has undermined it by suggesting that somehow the way the bond issue went was due to some Canadian policy. It was due basically to a nervousness in the market environment-
He said:
Maybe he would agree that he has a responsibility-
The Budget-Mr. Blenkarn
He was referring to me and for the first time I wondered how a poor country lawyer from the City of Mississauga was also all of a sudden responsible for the fact that a $750 million bond issue in Europe did not sell very well.
The government's policy has been to the blame the United States, to blame the provinces, to blame business, to blame Brian Peckford on one day, or Peter Lougheed on another day. On June 16, the government blamed me. All of a sudden, it was I who could not make things work, because the people did not have confidence in their government and its operations.
On that same date 1 forecast in the House of Commons that our deficit would be somewhere between $13 billion and $16 billion. On Monday night I could not believe my ears when I heard that our borrowing requirements were to be in excess of $17 billion and that our deficit would be $20 billion. I had no conception of how badly this government had mismanaged the affairs of Canada. It finally got to the point at which it had to come to the House of Commons on June 28 and tell us that it needed to borrow $17.1 billion, nearly three times what it said in November last would be its financial requirements.
I was first elected to this House of Commons on October 30, 1972. In that year, total government spending was $21,228 million. The total taxes taken in were $19,560 million and the deficit was $566 million. That was ten years ago. If we had kept within the range of inflation, this year's spending would possibly have reached $50 billion. Had we not been a little careful with spending, we might have reached a deficit of a billion dollars. Where are we going? Just ten years later our spending is $90 billion and our tax take is $70 billion. Where have these socialist policies, these N DP-oriented policies, taken us?
This is the party to my left which has been advocating certain policies to the Prime Minister and his colleagues. They are all the same type. They are the front runners for the Liberal Party. My western colleagues refer to the NDP as "Liberal Party West". Clearly it is the "Liberal Party West" because it does not have any member in what is traditionally called east of the Ottawa River, or eastern Canada. What do its members advocate? They have been advocating further state intervention in the lives of individuals, further government control.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Cutting taxes, stimulating the economy, industrial strategy!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What have we received from this government? We have received a whole series of these socially-oriented programs, programs designed for what was formerly called an industrial strategy. In 1972, that is what the leader of the NDP, the late David Lewis, called industrial strategy. So what we have received has been the EDP programs, I LAP programs, enterprise development programs and the DIP program.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tell that to the people at Admiral.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They once said they wanted housing programs, so we now have housing programs. We have the NIP

The Budget-Mr. Blenkarn
program, the CHIP program, the COSP program and all sorts of programs. My goodness gracious, one could write a book about the programs. Indeed, they do write books about the programs and send them around. They are well bound, but I do not think even those books contain all the programs. It would be impossible for a Member of Parliament to really understand all the various alphabet soup programs produced by this government, programs really designed for one purpose and one purpose only.
Let us talk about that purpose, because that is the essence of where we are and the problems we are experiencing. That purpose is to make individual Canadians more and more dependent upon government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Control the population.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The purpose is to take away, bit by bit, the individual economic freedom-making decision of individuals. I point out to Your Honour that when the freedom of people is taken away, their political freedom is taken away. That is why the New Democratic Party made sure that the right to own property was not in the Constitution.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, get out. That was provincial.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The NDP did not want it, and the Liberal Party did not want it because somewhere along the line some man would have gone to court and said, "I have a right to own my property and you cannot take it from me".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hon. members of the NDP do not like it when it is brought back to their attention. They do not like to be reminded-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is irrelevant.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -that the farmers of Saskatchewan, the voters of Saskatchewan, realized what the NDP had done with the right to property-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -how it operated a government which bought up all farmland and pushed up farm prices in Saskatchewan. That is why the NDP was thrown out.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why do you not attack those guys?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Take it easy on our friends!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My friend from Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher) says to take it easy on their friends in the NDP. We now have positive proof that the alliance is there-"take it easy on our friends".
We have a situation where we have had a whole series of economic programs that bit by bit control individuals. A builder may be afraid to criticize the government because he hopes Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation will give
him some money to finance a new apartment building in the form of a grant or interest-free loan.
Until recently a public servant was on my mailing list. When he was getting too much mail from me, his wife telephoned my constituency office. She asked that we take their name off the list. She said they support Mr. Blenkarn and are behind him 100 per cent, but are afraid the postman will note that they are always getting mail from him. They are worried that what happened to Neil Fraser might happen to them.
A chartered bank may be afraid to blow the whistle on this government because its guarantee for a loan may not come through. What is going to be the situation with Dome Petroleum?
An executive of an oil company may be worried about whether he will get his PIP grant on one basis or another. Perhaps he does not criticize.
An electrical manufacturer negotiating a foreign sale wants to make sure he receives his financing from the Export Development Corporation at a fancy low rate of interest which the minister and only the minister can supply. Maybe a volunteer organization would like to have a grant. Maybe a Portuguese club, an Italian newspaper or a senior citizens group are looking for a grant. Maybe it is a native person or a researcher at a university. 1 could go on and on.
These grant and aid programs bit by bit compromise people. They force people into making decisions. Bit by bit they leech away the political and economic freedom that Canadians have. Bit by bit they destroy vitality, entrepreneurship, drive and initiative because it is part of a program designed to bribe, cajole, manoeuvre and direct people from the ivory towers of Ottawa.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And build up a debt.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They do that for sure. What part does the budget play in this great control program? This budget is another giant step toward control. It imposes for the first time wage controls and wage guidelines on a mandatory basis at 6 per cent. It is a further control mechanism.
The budget provides for $3,000 grants to those who buy a new house and fill in the forms to prove that they paid some of their own cash. It is a further dependency. It proposes a program of 4 per cent interest related to small businesses that may want to expand. It subsidizes interest expense for those who do not have the ability to make their mortgage payments. Again and again and again it further intrudes into the decision-making process of individuals. Bit by bit it leeches away by these various measures, by the tiddley make-work programs and by tiddley grant programs, the freedom and capacity of Canada to compete in the world market.
I note, Mr. Speaker, you are ready to call it 5.45. I suggest we call it 5.45 for the bells.
